extracted.intended_audience: photojournalists, newspaper editors, and readers interested in photography ethics
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and newsroom policy guidance about acceptable digital editing for newspaper/photojournalistic images, and consequences for violations. Focuses on color alteration, 'toning', and the distinction between journalism and labeled art.

rubrics_metrics.name: No colors will be altered from the original scene photographed
rubrics_metrics.description: The Observer’s photo policy states: 'No colors will be altered from the original scene photographed.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy was applied to an image whose original sky was 'brownish-gray' but was 'enhanced with photo-editing software' to become 'a deep red' with a more distinct halo around the sun; such alterations violate the rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journalism cannot be about original art forms unless labeled as such
rubrics_metrics.description: As Observer editor Rick Thames explained: 'Journalism cannot be about original art forms, unless it’s labeled as such. Journalism is about capturing art in real life.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If equipment or tools fail (camera, notes, tape recorder), journalists should 'go back out the door and try to recapture that again' rather than attempting to recreate the scene in post-production; deviations must be explicitly labeled as art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition/limitation on 'toning' and similar manipulations that change scene perception
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Toning' is described as the act of darkening background elements so that foreground elements 'pop' off the page; this and similar manipulations were the subject of prior infractions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article situates digital toning relative to traditional darkroom practices (dodging and burning) and notes an ongoing debate in newspaper circles about how much digital editing is acceptable; manipulations that alter the factual appearance of the scene are treated as unacceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claimed intent to 'restore' color does not negate a policy violation
rubrics_metrics.description: Schneider said he 'did not intend to mislead readers, only to restore the actual color of the sky' after underexposing to offset sun glare.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Despite stated intent, the paper treated the alteration as a breach of policy and imposed sanctions; intent alone may not excuse departures from established photo policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: News organizations should have and enforce established photo-editing policies (with sanctions)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Observer had an established policy against altering color that was put in place specifically in response to previous infractions by the same photographer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enforcement actions cited include stripping of awards, reprimand, suspension without pay, and termination; the presence of a written policy and consistent enforcement are presented as essential to maintaining journalistic standards.
